newsitem.title: UK: IRA attack shows up hardline guerrilla stance.
newsitem.headline: IRA attack shows up hardline guerrilla stance.

text.p: The murder of two Northern Ireland policemen by Irish Republican Army (IRA) gunmen may be the product of divisions between hawks and doves among republicans seeking to end British rule in the province, analysts say.

The two policemen were shot in the head at point blank range on Monday in the town of Lurgan, south of Belfast, in an ambush which dealt a shattering blow to efforts to bring peace to Northern Ireland.

Britain and the Irish Republic say all the evidence points to a "bullet and ballot box" strategy by the IRA and its political ally Sinn Fein, and have challenged Sinn Fein to prove otherwise by condemning bombings and shootings.

But analysts said the ambush defied logic since it happened when frozen relations with Britain seemed to be thawing and Sinn Fein appeared closer than for many months to being allowed into multiparty talks on the province's future.

They said the attack pointed to internal divisions in the Republican Movement and a determination by hawks not to let negotiations compromise their fundamental aim of ending British rule in Northern Ireland and creating a united Ireland.

Richard English of Queen's University in Belfast, told Reuters: "I think what we are seeing is tension between two wings -- those who apparently believe they can make progress through politics and those who have always relied on force of arms."
The hawks seemed to have gone back to their "preferred methods because politics has not delivered what they want," he said.
"Political talks will always involve a compromise of their goals. If they are drawn into talks, that will force them to give up too much."
But analysts acknowledged it was very difficult for an outsider to work out the IRA's thinking.
"Everything is speculative," said political scientist Duncan Morrow of Belfast's University of Ulster. "It reminds me of Kremlinology."
"We know there are hawks. The question is: are there any doves? And were there ever any doves?"

With the IRA already accused of trying to foment a backlash by their foes in pro-British Protestant militias, analysts said the killing of the two policemen suggested hardliners among the guerrillas had decided violent confrontation was the only way to achieve their long term aims.

Sinn Fein, led by Gerry Adams, says all-party talks are the way to thrash out a new political settlement. That means face-to-face negotiations with representatives of the province's majority Protestants who despise republicanism and want to stay under British rule.
Britain says a Sinn Fein seat at the talks must be preceded by an unequivocal end to IRA violence.
Monday's shootings strangled an initiative by Briatin's new Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair to set in train low-level contacts with Sinn Fein even without an IRA ceaseire.
These fell well short of republican demands but nevertheless had been seen as offering some hope of a way out of 25 years of guerrilla strife.
Experienced political commentators said the killings bewildered many republican supporters and had taken British officials by surprise.
"The message seems to be that somebody in there does not want what Gerry Adams and the people around him say they want, which is speedy entry into talks," one commentator told Reuters.

The Irish News, Belfast's nationalist daily, reported that Catholic voters who helped Sinn Fein to significannt successes in local and British parliamentary elections in May felt betrayed because they had thought they were voting for a new peace.
